title: How to Survive in a World Without Rules
gist: Hal Brands argues the rules-based order is giving way not to anarchy but to a neoimperial, self-help world in which states must pay explicit risk premiums for resilience — chokepoint workarounds, strategic reserves, sovereign defense capacity — and warns that Trump is a symptom, not the cause, so no post-2028 snapback should be assumed. He frames seven survival rules, including that middle-power coalitions will fail and that revisionists like China may eventually regret losing freedom of navigation.

themes.theme: Risk premiums and the efficiency-to-resilience shift

insights.claim: The erosion of freedom-of-navigation norms mechanically raises shipping and insurance costs, disrupts supply chains and multiplies economic friction — a structural, not cyclical, cost increase for global trade.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Persistent upward pressure on freight and war-risk insurance rates should be treated as a regime change, not a spike to fade; favors shipping/tanker rate longs and companies with redundant logistics.
insights.quote: An era in which those norms crumble is one in which shipping and insurance costs shoot upward, supply chains are violently disrupted, and economic friction multiplies.
insights.locator: Fifth, if the dilemmas of the new era

insights.claim: Pipeline capacity that carries Gulf oil to market while bypassing the Strait of Hormuz is framed as an expensive but essential insurance policy that gradually reduces Iran's leverage.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Implies a multi-year capex cycle in Gulf bypass midstream infrastructure and a structural bid for pipeline/EPC contractors serving Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
insights.quote: An expanded pipeline network that brings Gulf oil to the world, while bypassing Hormuz, is an expensive but essential insurance policy
insights.locator: This makes workarounds—even cost-intensive ones

insights.claim: The weaponization of energy flows and critical minerals stocks requires a broad shift from efficiency to resilience, with prudent actors willingly paying a premium for insulation from coercion.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Structurally higher inventory levels and duplicated capacity compress margins broadly but create a persistent revenue stream for domestic/friendshored producers of minerals and energy.
insights.quote: prudent actors should be willing to pay a premium for insulation from coercive threats
insights.locator: Likewise, the weaponization of energy flows

insights.claim: As conflict disrupts food and energy distribution networks, even poor developing states will need to invest in larger strategic reserves — extending stockpiling demand well beyond rich-country buyers.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: A broadened, price-insensitive official bid for grains and fuels adds a persistent floor under soft commodity and refined product demand.
insights.locator: This applies, unfortunately, to poorer states as well

insights.claim: The recent Persian Gulf war demonstrated that the United States may lack the capability to uphold freedom of navigation in contested waters even when it has the will to do so.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Removes the implicit free option that a U.S. carrier group reopens any chokepoint; chokepoint disruptions should be priced with longer expected duration.
insights.quote: the United States may not have the ability to uphold freedom of navigation in contested waters, even when it summons the will
insights.locator: And as the recent Persian Gulf war has demonstrated

insights.claim: The emerging system is best modeled as a neoimperial age of overlapping spheres of influence rather than full-blown anarchy: China from the Himalayas to the East China Sea plus a digital sphere across the global south, Russia in Central Asia and Eastern Europe, Turkey and Israel carving up post-Assad Syria, and the United States claiming an entire hemisphere.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Country risk should be repriced by which sphere an asset sits in, not by global norms; assets on sphere boundaries carry the widest tail risk.
insights.quote: the rules-based order may be yielding to a neoimperial age
insights.locator: This isn’t full-blown anarchy

insights.claim: The United States has turned Venezuela into a vassal state and exacts tribute from allies around the Eurasian periphery — American behavior is presented as part of the revisionist trend, not a counterweight to it.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Allied sovereign and corporate planners must model the U.S. as a source of coercion risk, which supports hedging demand away from dollar-denominated dependence.
insights.quote: The United States has turned Venezuela into a vassal state and claimed an entire hemisphere as its domain. It exacts tribute from allies around the Eurasian periphery.
insights.locator: Then there’s Washington’s imperial restoration

insights.claim: Predatory enclosure of the seas is a single connected trend spanning China's South China Sea offensive, the Houthi Red Sea campaign, Russia's sovereignty claims over the Northern Sea Route, and Iran's Hormuz chokehold.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Treat maritime chokepoint events as correlated rather than idiosyncratic — a basket approach to shipping risk beats single-route hedging.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the norm that underpins global trade

insights.claim: Levels of state-based conflict have reached their highest mark in decades while arms control frameworks from U.S.-Russia nuclear agreements to land-mine accords are crumbling.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Supports a multi-year secular bid for defense primes and munitions capacity rather than a cyclical rearmament trade.
insights.quote: Levels of state-based conflict have reached their highest mark in decades.
insights.locator: Likewise, the global security environment grows more disordered

insights.claim: Trump is a symptom of deeper structural shifts — the insecurities of interdependence and resurgent great-power rivalry — so the world will not revert to a gentler state regardless of who wins in 2028 or 2032.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Positioning that assumes mean reversion in trade policy or alliance reliability after a U.S. election change is mispriced; structural fragmentation trades have a longer runway than the political cycle.
insights.quote: But whoever becomes president in 2028 or 2032, don’t expect that the world will revert to a fundamentally gentler state.
insights.locator: The first imperative is to recognize that nostalgia isn’t a strategy

insights.claim: Tariffs and other trade-distorting measures were already rising before Trump's 2025 tariff onslaught, and the WTO had been moribund for years — protectionism predates the current administration.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Trade-friction costs are a durable input to corporate margins; do not model them as a one-administration shock.
insights.quote: Tariffs and other trade-distorting measures were rising before U.S. President Donald Trump’s onslaught in 2025.
insights.locator: We’re a long way from a rules-based economy

insights.claim: European rearmament will not reach ambitious military spending targets unless countries pare back domestic entitlement programs that swelled while Washington covered much of NATO's cost.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Either European defense budget promises get cut, or European fiscal/political risk rises — watch entitlement reform as the leading indicator for whether defense order books actually convert.
insights.quote: Most countries won’t reach ambitious military spending targets unless they pare back domestic entitlement programs
insights.locator: Countries that root their mindsets in this new era

themes.theme: Self-help winners and the failure of middle-power coalitions

insights.claim: Poland and Japan are the models of successful self-help — historic defense investments that break old fiscal and political barriers, paired with new coalitions such as the Intermarium concept and Japan's quasi-alliances with Australia and the Philippines.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Polish and Japanese defense-industrial supply chains are the highest-conviction beneficiaries of the self-help regime, ahead of broader European names.
insights.quote: Poland and Japan are models: They are making historic defense investments that blow through old fiscal and political barriers.
insights.locator: Thus, a second rule: Self-help is vital

insights.claim: Mark Carney's Davos 'middle-power moment' will fail because no plausible middle-power coalition can contain China without U.S. support and key players like Brazil, India and Saudi Arabia see opportunity rather than danger in fragmentation.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Discount headlines about coordinated middle-power blocs defending trade rules; bilateral and small-group deals are where real flows shift.
insights.quote: If middle powers could set the terms of global order, they wouldn’t be middle powers.
insights.locator: This self-help surge illustrates a third principle

insights.claim: The realistic hedging path is smaller and more cohesive: Europe diversifying away from the U.S. market via India and Mercosur deals, Japan building Asian defense supply chains to cut technological dependence on Washington, and Canada deepening Arctic security cooperation with Scandinavia.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Watch EU-India and EU-Mercosur trade deals and intra-Asian defense procurement as concrete flow-shifting events rather than rhetoric.
insights.locator: It’s eminently reasonable for Europe to gradually reduce its reliance

insights.claim: Sustained self-help buys time for allies to consider more radical options including acquiring nuclear weapons, making proliferation a live medium-term scenario rather than a taboo.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Allied proliferation would be a discontinuous repricing event for regional risk assets; monitor Japanese and South Korean nuclear debate as a tail-risk indicator.
insights.quote: It also buys time to consider whether more radical forms of self-help, such as acquiring nuclear weapons, might one day be necessary.
insights.locator: This path—preserving as much cooperation as possible

themes.theme: AI, tech stack and transactional alliances

insights.claim: Even with the best AI models, the United States cannot dominate the AI age without allies occupying key nodes in the global tech stack, from the Netherlands to Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Chokepoint node owners — Dutch lithography and Taiwanese fabrication — retain structural bargaining power that limits how far Washington will squeeze them.
insights.quote: Washington may have the best artificial intelligence models, but it can’t dominate the AI age without the help of friends, from the Netherlands to Taiwan
insights.locator: Fourth, even as U.S. alliances become less special

insights.claim: The new alliance model will be explicitly transactional, exemplified by pacts trading allied support for AI supply chains in exchange for privileged access to U.S. computing power and frontier models.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Compute access is becoming a diplomatic currency — expect government-brokered allocation deals to shape where AI capacity and semiconductor capex land.
insights.quote: pacts that trade allied support in securing and strengthening AI supply chains for privileged access to U.S. computing power and frontier models
insights.locator: So the task for Washington and its allies

insights.claim: A transactional baseline of allied cooperation could still endure on rare-earth and semiconductor supply chains and the Western Pacific military balance, meaning fragmentation need not be total even in the harsher scenario.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Critical-minerals and chip cooperation is the most resilient piece of the alliance system — the last thing to break and the first to be rebuilt.
insights.locator: If this scenario materializes after Trump leaves office

insights.claim: China's trade-dependent economy still needs safe seas and foreign markets, so if the international economy fragments and freedom of navigation falters, Beijing may come to miss the rules-based order it helped dismantle.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Implies a ceiling on how far Beijing will push maritime disruption — useful for sizing tail risk in South China Sea and Taiwan scenarios.
insights.quote: If the international economy fragments and freedom of navigation falters, Beijing may miss the rules-based order after all.
insights.locator: Moreover, China’s trade-dependent economy

insights.claim: Mass rearmament triggered by autocratic aggression and an erratic America could leave Russia and China worse off — facing a heavily armed Japan unshackled from historical constraints and bulging Polish and German militaries no longer restrained by Washington.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: The second-order effect of U.S. retrenchment is a larger, less U.S.-dependent European and Asian defense market, structurally favoring local primes over U.S. exporters.
insights.quote: In a truly zero-sum era, everyone could end up less secure.
insights.locator: If countries concerned about aggressive autocracies

insights.claim: A gangster's ethos would rupture the relationships that magnify U.S. influence, giving other countries greater incentive to withhold cooperation or push back — legitimacy is treated as a direct input to American power.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Erosion of U.S. legitimacy is a slow-burn negative for dollar-system stickiness and for U.S. companies' access to allied markets.
insights.quote: Principle is a fount of power. If Washington forgets that, it will pay a heavy price.
insights.locator: U.S. support for a broadly beneficial order has lubricated its power

insights.claim: Trump reportedly proposed that Beijing, Moscow and Washington cooperate to paralyze the International Criminal Court, and after the January snatch of Nicolas Maduro declared that only his own morality — not international law or the U.S. Constitution — could constrain him.
insights.speaker: Hal Brands
insights.so_what: Legal-institutional constraints on U.S. action are weaker than models assume; expropriation, sanctions and extraterritorial action risk should be marked up for assets exposed to U.S. policy targets.
insights.quote: We live in a world … that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power
insights.locator: After ordering the January snatch of Venezuelan President
